entries.title: Say on screen when prices are delayed or invented
entries.body:
The engine announced SYNTHETIC whatever the source, so a screen fed by
Interactive Brokers still claimed to be simulated — and, worse, a screen fed
by ten-minute-old prices looked exactly like a live one. The real mode is now
carried through and broadcast the moment the engine starts, before a single
price is drawn.

Anything that is not live carries a banner naming it: delayed prices read
"DONNÉES DIFFÉRÉES ~10 MIN — NE PAS TRADER" in amber, invented ones "PRIX
SIMULÉS — AUCUN LIEN AVEC LE MARCHÉ". Only a genuinely live feed shows
nothing, so silence means live and never the reverse.

This is the same failure that had the platform showing a random walk under an
S&P 500 heading for days. The label is not decoration.

entries.title: Read real CME prices, and stop closing the socket before they arrive
entries.body:
Three faults stood between the engine and Interactive Brokers, each hiding
the next.

The connection was dropped the moment `subscribe` returned. Only that
function held the client, so the socket closed before a single tick landed
and the feed looked dead. The reading tasks now hold it for as long as they
read.

IBKR sends price and size in one combined tick far more often than as the
separate ticks the decoder expected, so the whole feed was discarded as
unrecognised. Both shapes are handled.

The probe had no log output at all, which is why "connected but silent" could
not be told apart from "connected, streaming, and decoded into nothing".
RUST_LOG now reveals every tick, and that is what identified the combined
form within one run.

Also adds the free delayed feed under IB_FEED_KIND, defaulting to REALTIME so
delayed prices are always asked for and never inherited. It names itself
"DIFFÉRÉ (~10 min)" wherever it surfaces: prices ten minutes old on a
scalping screen must be impossible to mistake for live ones.

MES now reads 7657.75 / 7658.25 from CME, with real book sizes.

entries.title: Name the Interactive Brokers accounts that actually exist
entries.body:
The account list was invented: DUA545090, U15525670 and a set of ctrader,
alpaca and paper entries corresponded to nothing, yet one carried a LIVE
badge. It read as a broker connection the platform did not have, and sent us
looking for a paper account that was never created.

It now names the real pair — U27457555 live, DUR611871 paper — with the ports
each Gateway listens on. They stay separate entries: live and paper are
different accounts and never share a number, and labelling one with the
other's identifier is how a test order reaches real money. The live entry is
deliberately unselectable, since nothing here trades live.

entries.title: Accept the timezone names a localised IB Gateway reports
entries.body:
A French Gateway announces "heure normale d'Europe centrale" instead of an
IANA name. The protocol layer rejects it and the connection fails with a
message about timezones surfaced as a refused connection — unreadable as the
locale problem it is, and it cost a debugging round on a setup that was
otherwise correct.

The known localised spellings are registered before connecting, so a French,
German or Spanish Gateway works with no environment variable to remember.

entries.title: Let the engine take its prices from Interactive Brokers
entries.body:
The IBKR adapter existed but only a standalone console probe used it. The
running platform drew every price from the synthetic generator, so the screen
labelled S&P 500 showed a seeded random walk with no relation to any exchange
— the operator's instinct caught this before the SYNTHETIC badge did.

TRADEVIEW_MARKET_SOURCE now selects the source, defaulting to SYNTHETIC so
nothing reaches a broker by accident. Under IBKR the engine subscribes
through the existing MarketDataProvider port, meaning the switch touches no
strategy, risk or execution code.

A failed connection is fatal rather than a fallback. Quietly reverting to
invented prices on a screen the operator believes is live is the worst
outcome available, so the engine refuses to start and says why.

Pausing gates the forwarder rather than the socket. The engine only acts on
what reaches it, so a halted market still cannot fill, without tearing down
and rebuilding a broker subscription on every toggle.

entries.title: Run the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq side by side
entries.body:
The platform simulated one instrument end to end. It now streams MES and MNQ
together, each with its own price profile: the Nasdaq sits near 25,000 and
moves three ticks a print against the S&P's one, so the two series no longer
look like the same index under different names. Seeds are derived per
instrument rather than shared, which would have made both indices move in
lockstep.

Every instrument gets its own analysis window. Blocks and steps describe a
single series, and pooling two would invent structure present in neither.

The front held a single symbol, a single price and a single analysis, so the
second stream silently overwrote the first. State is now keyed by instrument,
with the selected one exposed under the previous flat names so each view
stays explicit about which series it draws. Candles are filtered by
instrument as well as timeframe — the chart was already at risk of drawing
bars from a contract it was not labelled with.

Orders follow the instrument on screen, so a click cannot land on a series
the operator is not looking at.

Symbols come from TRADEVIEW_SYMBOLS; adding a third contract needs no code.

entries.title: Make the market play/pause control actually stop the feed, halted by default
entries.body:
The button only swapped its own icon. Data kept arriving whether it showed
play or pause, so a control that looked functional cut nothing — worse than
having no control, because it invites trust it does not earn.

Pausing now halts the generator at the source rather than freezing the
display. Freezing only the chart would leave the engine filling orders at
prices the operator cannot see, which is exactly the divergence this project
is built to avoid.

The feed starts halted. Opening the Market screen should not set a market
running by itself, and in SIM a running feed means fills.

MarketStatus carries feed_running, distinct from connected: the source is
reachable, it is simply not being consumed. The engine echoes the state after
each command so the button reflects what is actually running rather than what
the click hoped for, and the chart says plainly when the market is stopped.

Covered by tests asserting a halted feed delivers nothing and that resuming
restores it.

entries.title: Draw the block and step analytics on the chart, and make it zoomable
entries.body:
The analytics existed but nothing consumed them: the engine computed blocks
and steps and then dropped them on the floor. They are now broadcast as an
Indicators event in the same tagged shape as the market and execution
streams, and drawn — runs as shaded rectangles behind the bars, swings as a
polyline whose legs are labelled with their size in grid steps. Live runs and
unconfirmed pivots are dashed, since neither is settled yet.

Overlays are positioned by mapping each timestamp back to a bar index rather
than by assuming an offset, so an overlay cannot drift from the candles
beneath it.

Three defects surfaced while wiring this up:

- The chart stacked every timeframe at once. The engine emits candles for all
  five, and the front drew the lot, so 1-second bars sat on top of 5-minute
  ones. It now draws the timeframe the analytics declare.
- Worse, the front capped candles at 200 across all timeframes together. The
  1-second stream arrives five times more often and evicted the slower series
  the chart was drawing. The cap is now per timeframe.
- The synthetic feed moved up to six ticks per print, producing 15-second
  bars spanning 40 points. Real MES covers a point or two. One tick per print
  brings the step grid back from 25 points to 1.

Analysis runs on S15 by default rather than M5: a fresh session shows a
single M5 bar for its first five minutes, leaving nothing to analyse.
Configurable with TRADEVIEW_INDICATOR_TIMEFRAME.

Zoom is by wheel or by the +/- controls, and sets how many bars share the
canvas width.

entries.title: Run the platform on the S&P 500 alone, replacing the NVDA placeholder
entries.body:
The engine simulated NVDA while the product targets the S&P 500. Switching
the ticker alone would not have been enough: the synthetic feed walked a $211
share in cent increments with a $0.02 spread, which is not an index at 6,800
points however it is labelled, and every derived figure — spread, block
height, step grid — inherited those scales.

The price behaviour now lives in an InstrumentProfile, with a Micro E-mini
preset: quarter-point ticks, a one-tick spread, and moves drawn in whole
ticks. A real book never prints between ticks, and a sub-tick walk would hand
the indicators a precision that cannot exist.

The symbol is configuration (TRADEVIEW_SYMBOL), not a constant, and the
front-end reads the instrument the engine announces instead of naming one.
The order path previously sent "NVDA" hardcoded, so an order would have been
placed on an instrument the engine was not running.

entries.title: Add an Interactive Brokers market data adapter and a connection probe
entries.body:
First brick of the IBKR integration: a broker-ibkr crate implementing the
existing MarketDataProvider port, plus an ibkr-probe binary that proves the
engine can reach IBKR and read a live feed. No orders are placed.

The adapter goes behind the port defined in Phase 1 rather than into a new
parallel tree, so the engine still names no broker and swapping IBKR out
touches nothing else.

Three traps this encodes rather than leaves to be discovered at runtime:

- Gateway and TWS listen on different ports (4002/4001 versus 7497/7496).
  An unrecognised port is refused with both pairs named, instead of hanging
  until a timeout that says nothing.
- The contract month is resolved from the injected clock on the CME
  quarterly cycle. The library's own front_month() helper reads the wall
  clock and returns the next calendar month, which in July asks for an
  August MES — a contract that does not exist.
- A connected socket that never delivers is a distinct failure from a
  refused one, and is reported as such: outside CME hours, or without a
  data subscription, silence is what you get.

Quotes IBKR cannot express as a positive price are dropped with a warning
rather than forwarded, where they would poison the spread. Sizes fall back
to zero, since a bad size should not cost the quote.

Configuration is entirely environmental, documented in .env.example, so the
same binary runs locally or from Secrets Manager on AWS later.

entries.title: Add block and step analytics as an engine crate
entries.body:
Blocks (runs of same-direction candles) and steps (grid-quantised swings) are
strategy primitives, not chart decoration — an account named "blockfade"
trades the very runs the chart draws. Computing them in the engine keeps what
the operator sees and what a strategy would act on from drifting apart, and
respects the rule that no critical logic lives in TypeScript.

A step is modelled as a Decimal rather than a Price: it is a difference, and
Price rejects non-positive values by design. Likewise a block's range may
legitimately be zero.

Two behaviours worth stating, both covered by tests: a doji extends the run in
progress instead of splitting it, and a bar that sets a new extreme cannot
also confirm the reversal against that same extreme — otherwise one wide
candle would pivot against itself.

The step ladder reproduces the reference pairing, where a finest step of 0.63
at density 1 resolves to 0.50.

entries.title: Let the month recap collapse, and measure inception from the funded capital
entries.body:
The calendar can now be folded to its header, keeping the cards, chart and
win rate on one screen with no scrolling; the choice persists across reloads.

"Depuis le début" was measured against the first sample the page happened to
observe, so a reload reported +$0.00 while the balance clearly stood above
the funded amount. That period now comes from the engine's own figures —
funded capital and lifetime counters — which do not depend on how long the
browser has been watching. The shorter periods still derive from observed
samples, which is all that exists until the event store persists history.

entries.title: Fund the SIM account from configuration instead of a hardcoded $100,000
entries.body:
The starting capital was written into the server as 100_000, which did not
match the account being modelled. It now defaults to 39,000 and can be set
with TRADEVIEW_INITIAL_CAPITAL; a value that is not a positive number aborts
startup rather than quietly reverting to a default, since a wrong balance
silently distorts every percentage on the dashboard.

The account id no longer embeds the amount, the reset button label reads the
figure from the engine rather than repeating it, and the front-end placeholder
shown before the first account message matches.

entries.title: Make dashboard period filters real, and keep the calendar clear of the chart
entries.body:
The week/month/year/all buttons only trimmed the chart before; every other
figure still covered the whole session. Each period now derives its own
metrics by differencing the cumulative counters against the last sample
taken before the window opens, so result, return, win rate, average per day
and traded days all follow the selection. The calendar dims days outside the
active period rather than showing an unrelated month.

"This week" now means since Monday, not the last seven days — likewise month
and year are calendar periods, which is what the labels claim.

The top band (capital and result cards, chart, stats) is given a fixed
minimum height and cannot shrink, so the calendar sits strictly below it and
is reached by scrolling instead of crowding the chart.

Axis labels were rounding to the same value: a $10 move on a $100k account
printed "$100.1k" three ticks in a row. Decimal places are now chosen from
the span on screen.

entries.title: TradeView dashboard: capital curve, daily PnL calendar, brand colours
entries.body:
Adds the SILO-style capital curve (Recharts area chart, right-hand axis,
current-value marker) and a month calendar of daily results below it, so
scrolling down shows previous days' profit. Both read only real engine
data: days without executions stay visibly empty rather than being filled
with invented figures, since the event store is still in-memory and holds
no history until Phase 3 adds persistence.

Colours now come from the logo, sampled from tv.png: blue #789CFC for a
gain, violet #A854FC for a loss, applied to the dashboard, the header PnL
badge and the Market candles. Status colours (LIVE/DEMO/SIM, connection,
ACTIVE) are left alone — they signal environment, not direction.

Hover detail gives exact figures rather than k-rounded ones, on the curve,
the capital and result cards, and every calendar day.

Two defects fixed along the way:

- Orders placed from the UI never reached the engine. The hook stacked
  WebSockets on React re-mounts and stale reconnect timers, so `wsRef`
  often pointed at a CONNECTING socket while `placeOrder` dropped the
  send in silence. Connections are now deduplicated, intentional closes
  no longer trigger a reconnect, and a send that cannot go out surfaces
  as an error. The engine side also logs malformed commands instead of
  discarding them.

- The sidebar is position:fixed, so the workspace started at x=0 and slid
  underneath it, hiding 280px of every view — including the Market order
  panel.

entries.title: Add TradeView front-end components, WebSocket hook and env template
entries.body:
These files existed only on disk and had never been committed: the five
TradeView views (header, account selector, dashboard, market, data), the
useTradeViewWebSocket hook, and the .env.example template documenting the
Supabase and Rust engine variables.

Also includes the in-progress App.tsx and TradeViewPage.tsx changes and a
.claude/launch.json describing how to start the dev server.
